quiz.p: Which of these is a water habitat?
quiz.why: A temple tank holds water where fish, frogs and lotus live. The others are not water habitats.
Sea water is salty, about 35 grams of salt in every litre. Ponds, rivers and rain are fresh.

quiz.p: Priya warms three glasses of water: fridge-cold tap water, fridge-cold boiled water, and room-temperature tap water. Which grows the most bubbles?
quiz.why: Cold water holds the most dissolved air, so most comes out when it warms. Boiling had already driven the air out of the boiled water.

quiz.p: What were the tiny bubbles on the inside of the warmed glass?
opts: Air that had been dissolved in the water
quiz.why: Nothing was added. The air was dissolved in the water all along and came out as the water warmed.

opts: Air from above the water, always
quiz.why: A fish's gills take the dissolved oxygen out of the water. Picking 'the water itself' is a very common mistake.

quiz.p: Why might fish gulp at a pond's surface on a hot morning?
opts: The water is short of oxygen
They want to see the sun
quiz.why: Warm water holds less oxygen, and at night algae make none. By morning the oxygen is low, so fish gulp the water at the top.
A tadpole breathes dissolved oxygen with gills. As they become a frog, lungs grow and the gills go.

quiz.p: Why must a frog's skin stay wet?
opts: Because they breathe through their skin, and oxygen passes only through wet skin
quiz.why: A frog breathes partly through their skin. Dry skin cannot take in oxygen.

quiz.p: What are the holes in a lotus stem for?
opts: Carrying air down to the parts in the mud
quiz.why: Pond mud has almost no oxygen. Air canals carry air from the leaves to the underground stem and roots.
Algae photosynthesise, which needs light. In the dark they make none but still use some.

quiz.p: A lake gets sewage flowing into it, and it turns bright green. Why do fish start to die?
opts: The green colour hurts their eyes
Far too many algae grow, then die and rot, and the rotting uses up the oxygen
quiz.why: Sewage feeds an algal bloom. When the algae die, bacteria rot them and use up the oxygen fish need.

quiz.p: Arjun puts cucumber slices in very salty water. Why do they go floppy?
opts: Water moves out of them into the salty water
They soak up too much water
quiz.why: Water moves from the less salty side to the more salty side. The cucumber lost water and went limp.

quiz.p: Why can't most river fish live in the sea?
opts: The salty sea would pull water out of their bodies
There is no food in the sea
quiz.why: A river fish's body is much less salty than the sea, so they would keep losing water, like the cucumber.

items.p: Which of these is a water habitat?
items.why: A pond is a water habitat, a home in water for fish, frogs, lotus and algae. A desert, a tree trunk and a cave are land habitats.

items.p: Sort these water habitats. Is the water fresh or salty?
items.why: Ponds, rivers, tanks and rain are fresh water, with very little salt. The seas are salt water.

items.p: A fish breathes the water itself.
items.why: False. A fish breathes the oxygen dissolved in the water. Its gills take that oxygen out of the water.

items.p: Cold water holds more dissolved air than warm water.
items.why: True. That is why the fridge-cold glass grew the most bubbles as it warmed up.

items.p: Meena fills a glass with cold water from the fridge and leaves it on the table. An hour later, tiny bubbles cover the inside of the glass. What are the bubbles?
opts: Air that was dissolved in the water
items.why: The water held dissolved air. As it warmed up, it could not hold it all, so some came out as bubbles. Steam comes only from very hot water.

items.p: A fish takes oxygen out of the water with their ____.
items.why: Gills have many thin red folds full of blood. Oxygen passes from the water into the blood there.

items.p: A young frog that lives in water and has a tail is called a ____.
items.why: A tadpole breathes with gills. They grow legs and lungs, and their tail shrinks, as they become a frog.

items.p: A grown-up frog breathes with their lungs and with their...
items.why: Oxygen passes through a frog's thin skin, but only when the skin is wet. That is why frogs stay near water.

items.p: Why does a lotus stem have holes running through it?
opts: To carry air down to the parts in the mud
items.why: Pond mud has almost no oxygen. The holes are air canals that carry air from the leaves down to the underground stem and roots.

items.p: Match each living thing to how they get their oxygen.
pairs: air sent down through the stem
items.why: Each living thing in a pond has their own way of getting oxygen.

items.p: Algae make food and oxygen in sunlight.
items.why: True. Algae photosynthesise like plants. In the dark they stop making oxygen.

items.p: Ravi puts cucumber slices in very salty water. After 20 minutes, what happens to them?
items.why: Water moves out of the cucumber into the saltier water, so the slices go limp. Sea water would do the same to a river fish.

items.p: Put a frog's life in order.
items.why: A frog hatches from an egg as a tadpole, grows legs, loses their tail and becomes a frog.

items.p: Why do fish in a pond sometimes gulp at the surface just before sunrise? Use the words 'algae' and 'oxygen'.
items.a: At night, algae cannot make oxygen, but everything in the pond keeps using it. By sunrise the oxygen is lowest, so fish gulp the water at the top, which touches the air.
items.why: A full answer says that algae stop making oxygen at night and that the oxygen gets used up.

items.p: Draw a pond. Show a lotus, a frog, a fish and some algae, each in the part of the pond where they live.
items.a: Lotus leaves above the water with roots in the mud, a frog at the edge, a fish in the water and algae near the top, where the light is.
items.why: Each living thing lives where they get what they need.
items.art: A blank outline of a pond with its bank, water and muddy bottom.

items.p: In the Flat or Tall test, which dough shape stayed put when water was poured at it?
items.why: The flat dome is low, so the water slides over it, and its wide base grips the plate. Many stream animals are flat for this reason.

items.p: In the Cold Glass Test, why did glass B, the boiled water, grow almost no bubbles?
opts: Boiling had already driven most of the air out
Glass B was a different shape
items.why: Boiling drives dissolved air out of water. The full, capped bottle stopped much air dissolving back in. So there was little air left to come out.

items.p: In the Cold Glass Test, what was the one thing that changed between the three glasses?
items.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. Here it was the water inside: cold tap, cold boiled or room-temperature tap.

items.p: A fish can breathe in air, as long as their gills stay in the air.
items.why: False. Out of water, a fish's thin gill folds stick together and stop working, so most fish cannot breathe in air. A few, like the murrel, have extra air-breathing parts.

items.p: Water holds about how much oxygen compared with the same amount of air?
items.why: Water holds about 30 times less oxygen than the same amount of air. That is why fish must pass so much water over their gills.

items.p: At what time of day does a green pond usually have least oxygen?
items.why: Algae make oxygen only in light. All night, everything uses oxygen and none is made, so it is lowest just before sunrise.

items.p: When far too many algae grow in a lake, often because of sewage, it is called an algal ____.
items.why: In an algal bloom the water turns thick and green. When the algae die and rot, the oxygen can run out.

items.p: A lake near a city turns bright green and many fish die. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Sewage or fertiliser feeding too many algae
items.why: Sewage and fertiliser feed algae. When the huge bloom dies, bacteria rot it and use up the oxygen the fish need.

items.p: Salty water is heavier than the same amount of fresh water.
items.why: True. That is why fresh water floated on top of salty water in the layers activity.

items.p: A sea fish keeps losing water to the salty sea. What do they do about it?
opts: It drinks sea water and pushes the salt out through its gills
They swim to a river every night
items.why: Sea fish drink sea water to replace the water they lose. Their gills push the extra salt back out.

items.p: A river fish has the opposite problem. Water keeps soaking into their body. What do they do?
opts: They make a lot of very watery urine
items.why: Fresh water keeps soaking into a river fish, so their body gets rid of the extra as lots of very watery urine.

items.p: Water that is a mix of fresh and salt water, where a river meets the sea, is called ____ water.
items.why: The Kerala backwaters, Pulicat lake and Chilika lake are partly brackish.

items.p: Why do frogs come out after rain?
opts: The rain washes their food away
The air is damp, so their skin stays wet for breathing
items.why: A frog breathes partly through their skin, which must stay wet. Damp air after rain lets it move about without drying out.

items.p: Match each problem to the feature that helps.
pairs: air canals in the lotus stem
a flat body that hugs rocks
items.why: Each feature solves a problem that the living thing has in water.

items.p: Explain why fish in the story of Kavya's pond stopped gulping at dawn after the rain.
items.a: The rain cooled the water, and cool water holds more oxygen. The wind and splashing rain mixed more air into the water.
items.why: Two reasons are best: cooler water and air mixed in by waves and rain.

items.p: In the water plant activity, the sprig in the cupboard made few or no bubbles. What does this tell us?
opts: Plants make oxygen only in light
Water in cupboards has no air
items.why: Plants and algae need light to photosynthesise. In the dark they make no oxygen.

items.p: A fish tank sits in a sunny window in May, and the fish keep gulping at the top. What is the best fix?
opts: Move it into the shade and add an air pump or more plants
Turn off the light at night
items.why: Shade keeps the water cooler, so it holds more oxygen. A pump mixes in air, and plants add oxygen in the day.

items.p: Two ponds are the same size. Pond A is clear and cool under trees. Pond B is shallow, sunny and very green. Which is more likely to run short of oxygen at dawn?
items.why: Pond B is warmer, so it holds less oxygen. Its many algae use up oxygen all night. So at dawn it has the least.

items.p: Glass A had cold tap water and grew many bubbles. Glass C had room-temperature tap water and grew fewer. What does this show?
opts: Cold water held more air to begin with
items.why: Both glasses were warmed the same way. The cold water started with more dissolved air, so more came out.

items.p: A warm aquarium can hold more fish than a cool one of the same size.
items.why: False. Warm water holds less oxygen, so a warm tank can support fewer fish, not more.

items.p: Why do fish in a river usually face upstream?
opts: So water flows into their mouths and over their gills the right way
items.why: Facing the current, water flows in at the mouth and out over the gills. Facing the other way, water would push against the gill covers.

items.p: A girl says, 'Green water is always bad for fish.' Is she right? Explain.
items.a: Not always. Some algae feed the animals in a pond and make oxygen in the day. The trouble comes when far too many grow, and they use up oxygen at night and when they rot.
items.why: A good answer says some algae are good and too many are harmful.

items.p: The hilsa lives in the sea and lays their eggs in rivers. What must their body be able to do?
opts: Live in both salty and fresh water
items.why: Moving from the sea to a river, the hilsa must cope with very different saltiness. Most fish cannot do this.

items.p: Kavya's Thatha said the murrel did not mind the shortage of oxygen. Why?
opts: They can breathe air at the surface
items.why: The murrel has extra air-breathing parts above its gills, so it can gulp air when the water is short of oxygen.

items.p: A lotus leaf stands high above the water. The plant's roots are in mud. Explain how air gets from the leaf to the roots.
items.a: Air goes into the leaf and travels down long air canals inside the leaf stalk and underground stem to the roots in the mud.
items.why: The answer should name the air canals, the tubes you saw as holes in the stem.

items.p: Tiny algae in the sea make about how much of the oxygen made on Earth each year?
items.why: Algae and other tiny ocean life make about half. Land plants make most of the rest.

items.p: Put the pond's day in order, starting at sunset.
items: Noon: algae making lots of oxygen
All night: everything keeps using oxygen
a: All night: everything keeps using oxygen
Noon: algae making lots of oxygen
items.why: Oxygen falls all night, is lowest at dawn, and rises again once the sun shines on the algae.

items.p: Why can't we drink sea water when we are thirsty?
opts: It is so salty that it pulls more water out of our body
items.why: Sea water is saltier than our blood. Drinking it makes our body lose water to get rid of the salt, just as the cucumber lost water.

items.p: The Cold Glass Test shows that nothing at all is hidden in clear water.
items.why: False. The bubbles that appeared showed that air was dissolved in the water, out of sight.

maths.problem: In the Cold Glass Test, Lakshmi counted the bubbles on the bottom of each glass after 15 minutes. Glass A had 48 bubbles. Glass C had 12 bubbles. How many times as many bubbles did glass A have?
maths.explain: Glass A had 48 bubbles and glass C had 12. 48 divided by 12 is 4. So glass A had 4 times as many. Check: 12 + 12 + 12 + 12 = 48.
maths.context: This is about the Cold Glass Test. You warm three glasses of water in a warm bath and count the bubbles of air that come out.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'more bubbles' tells us little. Dividing shows how many times more air came out of the colder water.

maths.problem: Sea water has about 35 grams of salt in every litre. A bucket holds 10 litres of sea water. About how much salt is in it?
maths.explain: Each litre has about 35 grams. 10 litres have 10 times as much. 35 times 10 is 350. So about 350 grams, which is about as heavy as a small packet of salt.
maths.context: This is about how salty the sea is. Every litre of sea water has about 35 grams of salt dissolved in it.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying turns a small number we can't picture into a big one we can, like a whole packet of salt in one bucket.

maths.problem: In the Day and Night token game, the pond starts with 8 oxygen tokens. Three fish and the algae and snails use 4 tokens every round. Two NIGHT cards come in a row, adding nothing. How many tokens are left after the two nights?
maths.explain: Each round uses 3 tokens for the fish and 1 for the algae and snails, so 4. After the first night, 8 - 4 = 4 are left. After the second, 4 - 4 = 0. The fish must gulp at the surface. One more night would leave them short.
maths.context: This is about the Day and Night in the Pond game, where tokens stand for the oxygen in the water.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting round by round lets us predict exactly when the pond would run out, before it happens.

maths.problem: Kavya's water bath started at 40 degrees. After 15 minutes it was 34 degrees. By how many degrees did it cool? If it kept cooling at the same speed, what would it be after another 15 minutes?
maths.answer: It cooled by 6 degrees. After another 15 minutes it would be about 28 degrees.
maths.explain: 40 - 34 = 6, so it cooled 6 degrees in 15 minutes. Another 15 minutes at the same speed would take off another 6: 34 - 6 = 28. Really, warm water cools more slowly as it gets near room temperature, so it might stay a little warmer.
maths.context: This is about the warm water bath in the Cold Glass Test. Suppose Kavya put a kitchen thermometer in the bath to see how fast it cooled.
maths.why_maths: Finding the pattern in two readings helps us guess the next one, and then check whether the guess was right.

maths.problem: A frog's tadpole stage lasts about 8 weeks. How many days is that? If a tadpole hatched on the 1st of July, about when would they become a frog?
maths.explain: A week has 7 days. 8 times 7 is 56. July has 31 days, so after 1st July, 30 days take us to the 31st of July. 56 - 30 = 26 more days takes us to about the 26th of August. Different frogs take different times, and warm water makes tadpoles grow faster.
maths.context: This is about the frog's life cycle. A tadpole lives in water for some weeks before they become a frog.
maths.why_maths: Counting on a calendar tells us when to look for young frogs after the monsoon begins.

roots.context: We have learned that water holds dissolved air, and how fish, frogs, lotus and algae live on it. Now we ask what life in water tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your cold glass of water grew bubbles as it warmed, though nothing was added. That air had been dissolved in the water all along, out of sight. Fish breathe that dissolved oxygen through their gills. Warm water holds less, so on a hot, still night a pond can run short of oxygen for its fish.
deep_truth.habit: We think of water and air as two separate worlds: air is for breathing, and water is where you cannot breathe. But every pond, river and sea has air dissolved in it, and that is what its fish and tadpoles breathe.
deep_truth.evidence: Glass A, cold tap water, grew many bubbles as it warmed. Glass B, boiled water, grew almost none. Fish breathe that same dissolved oxygen, and measurements since 1809 show it falling as they breathe.

three.who_am_i: You breathe air with lungs. A fish breathes the same oxygen, dissolved in water, with gills.
three.what_is_life: A tadpole breathes with gills, then grows into a frog that breathes with lungs and skin. One life can change how they breathe.
three.what_is_this_world: Tiny algae floating in the sea make about half of the oxygen made on Earth each year.

roots.thread: A pond holds one store of dissolved air. Algae and water plants add oxygen to it in sunlight. Fish, tadpoles, snails and the plants themselves take from it all day and all night. So many different lives breathe from the same water, the way a whole family breathes the air of one room. When the store runs low, every one of them feels it.

science.text: Water holds dissolved oxygen, and cold water holds more than warm water. At fridge-cold, water holds almost twice as much as on a hot afternoon.
Algae and other tiny living things in the sea make about half of the oxygen made on Earth each year.
What fish feel when they are hurt is still argued about by scientists.

other_view.view: A pond is not one family breathing together. Each fish, plant and microbe takes what they need for themselves, and they compete for space, food and oxygen. The sharing is a result of chemistry, not of anyone choosing to share.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home, with the materials listed. The Cold Glass Test needs only glasses, two bottles, a fridge and a warm bath. Fridge-cold water reliably grows tiny bubbles on its sides within 10 to 15 minutes in a bath that feels warm on the wrist. The boiled water is chilled in a bottle filled to the top, so little air dissolves back in, and it grows almost none. The step says what to do if nothing appears: add a little hot water and wait 10 more minutes, and use a torch from the side. The salty cucumber uses 2 tablespoons of salt in a cup, much saltier than the sea, so the slices go clearly floppy in 20 minutes. A sea-strength bowl is included, and the step says honestly that its change may be small. The flat or tall test is done over the sink with atta dough and a steel plate on a book. The lotus stem activity needs thamarai thandu or kamal kakdi from a market, and gives a straw and a photo as the fallback, so it is not in the spine. Hydrilla costs a few rupees at an aquarium shop, so its activity is outside the spine too. The green water jar is covered with cloth so mosquitoes cannot breed in it, and it gives a fix if no algae grow in three weeks. Both games work for one child. The spine fits about 90 minutes over two sessions.

how_we_found_out.story: About 2,400 years ago in Greece, the thinkers Anaxagoras and Diogenes of Apollonia said that fish breathe air out of the water through their gills. Aristotle disagreed. He wrote that fish do not breathe at all, and that the water over their gills only cools them. Much later, after chemists found in the 1780s that water is made of hydrogen and oxygen, some people guessed that fish split the water itself to get its oxygen. In 1809, in Paris, the explorer Alexander von Humboldt and the chemist Provençal tested this. They kept fish in closed jars of water and measured the gases dissolved in the water before and after. The dissolved oxygen went down, and carbon dioxide went up, just as when we breathe air. So fish do breathe, and they breathe the oxygen dissolved in water, not the water. Anaxagoras had been close to right all along.
how_we_found_out.who: Alexander von Humboldt, a German explorer and scientist, and Provençal, a French chemist, with the older ideas of Anaxagoras, Diogenes of Apollonia and Aristotle
how_we_found_out.when: About 400 BCE (the Greek ideas) and 1809 (the measurements in Paris)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Aristotle thought fish do not breathe and that the water only cools their gills. Later, some people thought fish split water to get oxygen. Humboldt and Provençal measured the gases in the water and showed that fish take out the dissolved oxygen and give out carbon dioxide.
